CHAPTER III ALTERNATIVES
A. The Alternatives Considered
A thorough consideration of all of the alternatives available to the proposed Randolph project can be defined in the following categories; 1. "No Action" could be taken, 2. The type and size of the project could be reduced, or 3. The location of the project could be moved.
1. "No Action could be taken:
No action could be taken with the Randolph project. With a no action solution the several million dollars of scheduled funds could be used in other areas. No relocation would be needed. No program or rehabilitation or redevelopment would exist. This is not to say that all problems would cease and desist. The Downtown Expressway would (as proposed) be built. Deterioration would continue. Citizen-governmental ties would deteriorate. Randolph is a result of neglect. Further lack of action may well antagonize the citizens in the neighborhood, particularly in view of the time and energy spent in the citizen participation process for this renewal proposal. A continuation of the "no action" policy can therefore be expected to result in considerable citizen reaction.
2. The Type and Size of the Project could be Changed:
Limiting the scope of the Randolph project could be achieved by elimination of the rehabilitation program and area. Basically the Randolph area is composed of three distinct sections; one section to be entirely redeveloped, one section to be completely rehabilitated (with the possibility of spot clearance), and the last section to be treated by a combination of redevelopment and rehabilitation. Elimination of rehabilitation areas would reduce the size of the project by approximately two-thirds and eliminate the need for rehabilitation loans and services. The project area would be a total clearance area. The proposed plan could still be implemented and blighting influences within the redevelopment area removed. Noise and light intrusions from the proposed Downtown Expressway could be modified by the physical design of the plan, and by additional sound barriers, mounds, walls, and/or landscape treatments. Relocation would not be affected, the same numbers of residents would still require housing. Street patterns could remain approximately as proposed.
